The Upanishad of Vision.
"May they swell"—thus the Peace.
First Section.
The means for liberation while living is the eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga).
The great yogi Dattātreya is the Lord who brings all beings into existence;
he is the four-armed Mahāviṣṇu, consecrated in the sovereignty of yoga. (1)
His disciple, an excellent sage named Sāṃkṛti, who was full of devotion,
questioned his teacher in private with palms joined in reverence and endowed with humility.
O Blessed One, tell me the Yoga with its eight limbs and its full exposition,
by the mere knowledge of which I may become liberated while living.
O Sāṃkṛti, listen; I shall explain the Yoga consisting of the eight limbs.
This is the exposition [of the means] for awakening to Brahman alone through the eight limbs of Yoga, beginning with *yama*.
I worship that state of absolute liberation (kaivalya) which yogis attain.

Indeed, here unfolds this *Darśanopaniṣad*, which is divided into sections of the Samaveda; it is intent upon revealing the eight-limbed yoga beginning with *yama*—accompanied by the knowledge of the non-dual Brahman—and culminates in the realization of Brahman alone, free from all opposition. Of this [Upanishad], from its brief text...
The commentary begins.
This narrative, consisting of questions and answers between Sāṃkṛti and Dattātreya, is for the purpose of praising this knowledge.
He introduces the narrative with the words: "Dattātreya... (1–2). Why? "O Blessed One," [he asks].
And so forth. Thus questioned by Sāṃkṛti, the Blessed One said: "O Sāṃkṛti... and so on.
The summary of the eight limbs: restraint (yama), observance (niyama), and likewise posture (āsana). || 4 ||
O Brahmin, likewise there is prāṇāyāma, and after that pratyāhāra;
then dhāraṇā, as well as dhyāna, and samādhi is the eighth, O sage.
He asks, "Which are the eight limbs? and replies: "Restraint (yama) and so forth. (4–5)
The tenfold restraint consists of:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, straightforwardness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity; these are the ten restraints (yamas). (6)
He states the tenfold division of the limbs of *yama* as follows: "Non-violence," and so forth. (6)
O ascetic, apart from the method prescribed in the Vedas, there is no non-violence;
for violence committed through body, mind, or speech is indeed violence, and not otherwise. (7)
O Sage, that understanding which holds that the Self is omnipresent, indivisible, and ungraspable is declared by the knowers of Vedānta to be the supreme non-violence.

He states the ten-fold set of virtues characterized by non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth, according to the distinction between the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*), beginning with the word "vede" (in the Veda).
The meaning is that the violence toward animals and other creatures prescribed in the sacrifices mentioned in the Veda is indeed non-violence. Or else, [he speaks of] "ātma" and so forth.
O Lord of Sages, O Brahmin, that which is seen, heard, or smelled by the senses such as the eyes is indeed true;
its description shall be true and cannot be otherwise.
(154) The conviction that "Brahman alone is the supreme truth and nothing else" is declared as that supreme truth by those who have reached the further shore of the knowledge of Vedānta. || 10 ||
The definition of the truth of means and the goal is as follows: "The eye," and so forth. (9.25)
Non-stealing is the cessation from taking what belongs to another—whether it be a blade of grass, a jewel, gold, or even a pearl—from the mind; this is what the wise know as non-stealing. (11)
O great sage, that which is devoid of worldly transaction through the perception of non-self within the self is called non-stealing by the knowers of the Self. 12.
Celibacy consists of avoiding women in body, speech, and mind; when one approaches one's own wife only during her season, that is called celibacy. (13)
O scorcher of foes, the movement of the mind toward the state of Brahman is celibacy;
compassion toward all beings as toward one's own self, through body, mind, and speech, is likewise [celibacy].
That which is called *anujñā* (consent) by the knowers of Vedānta is indeed compassion (*dayā*),
which consists in constant straightforwardness toward one's son, friend, wife, enemy, and oneself. (15)
O Sage, that which is called "straightness" by me is of a single form:
it is forbearance through body, mind, and speech when one is tormented by enemies. (16)
O bull among sages, that cessation of the agitation of the intellect is forbearance;
steadfastness is liberation from the Vedas and non-Vedas [dualistic knowledge], and not otherwise from the cycle of existence. (17)
Thus, the accomplishment of consciousness is declared by the knowers of the Vedas to be fortitude;
it is the mind that remains unshaken in the realization: "I am the Self, and I am not another. (18)
Moderate diet consists of eating little and eating what is refined; it is that which leaves a fourth part remaining.
Therefore, eating in accordance with the requirements of yoga is called moderate eating. (19)
O Great Sage, purity consisting of the removal of the impurities of one's own body by means of earth and water is known as external purity; they know that mental purity is right reflection.
The wise say that the knowledge "I am pure" is true purity;
for the body is extremely impure, while the embodied soul is utterly stainless. (21)
Having understood the difference between these two, for whom is purification ordained?
That man who, abandoning the purification of knowledge, delights in the external, [is truly impure]. (22)
O observer of noble vows, that fool abandons gold and grasps a clod of earth;
[so it is for one who has attained the method of knowing the Self as Brahman]—for the yogin who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished all that was to be done. (23)
There is nothing further to be done; if there were something to be done, one would not be a knower of reality.
For those who have realized the Self, there is nothing whatsoever to be done even within the three worlds.
Therefore, O Sage, with every effort through the means of non-violence and the like, know the Self as the imperishable Brahman through the realization born of knowledge. 25.
Thus ends the first section;
the second section is on the tenfold discipline.
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord, listening to the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation of mantras, and observance of vows. (1)
These restraints (niyamas) have been declared; I shall describe them in order, so listen.
He states the tenfold divisions of the limbs of the restraints, beginning with "tapa" (austerity). || 1 ||
Austerity (tapaḥ) consists of performing penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa according to the methods prescribed in the Vedas. || 2 ||
That which is the withering of the body is called "penance" by the wise.
What is liberation? How and by whom was the cycle of existence entered? (3)
Thus, the wise who understand the true meaning praise austerity (*tapas*).
He describes the characteristics of the rules for austerity and so forth, according to the distinction between the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*), beginning with the word "Veda": (2-10, p.
157). Contentment (*saṃtoṣaḥ*).
The constant joy that arises in men from obtaining things by chance; || 4 ||
The wise, who are solely intent upon thorough knowledge, recognize that as true contentment which one obtains through detachment from everything up to the vision of Brahman.
One who is free from attachment everywhere knows supreme contentment;
faith in what is prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti— that which is trust— is called *āstikya*.
Giving wealth acquired by righteous means with faith to a weary person belonging to the Vedic community,
or whatever else is bestowed, that is called "giving" (dāna) by me.
Worship of the Lord is that action which is free from passion and the like, whose heart is not corrupted by falsehood and such through speech, and which is devoid of violence and other such acts. (8)

The wise person should understand that the hearing of the Vedānta— the hearing of the established conclusion— is Truth, Knowledge, the Infinite, the Supreme Bliss, the Ultimate, the Eternal, and the Inner Self (pratyak). 9.
Whatever action may be contemptible within the paths of the Vedas or the world, that sense of shame one feels toward it is proclaimed as *hrī*. 10.
That conviction which one has toward all Vedic matters should be considered true wisdom;
even when instructed by a teacher, one remains free from attachment to them.
Even if a path contrary to the Vedas is taught by a guru, one who is devoid of attachment to it should perform only the practices prescribed in the Vedas; this is the meaning. (11–16)
Japa is defined as the practice of mantra according to the very path prescribed in the Vedas,
as found in the Kalpasūtras, the Vedas, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Purāṇas.
And that mode of conduct which exists in the Itihāsas is called "japa" by me;
indeed, japa is said to be of two kinds: vocal and likewise mental.
Vocal [recitation] is proclaimed to be of two kinds: whispered and loud;
mental [recitation] relies on a twofold division based on the distinction between reflection and meditation. (14)

It is said that whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is a thousand times more effective than loud recitation (uccaiḥ), and likewise, mental recitation (mānasa) is said to be a thousand times more effective than whispered recitation. || 15 ||
(159) For all [practitioners], loud recitation shall yield the fruit as described;
however, if the mantra is heard by the ear, even if whispered, it becomes fruitless. (16)
Thus ends the second section.
The third section: the nine seats.
The Svastika, Gomukha, Padma, Vīra, and Siṃhāsana postures, as well as Bhadra, Muktāsana, and Mayūrāsana. || 1 ||

O bull among sages, having described the characteristics of the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), he states the characteristics of the postures (āsanas), beginning with the ninth, known as *sukhāsana*, in the words "the Svastika," and so forth.
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs, one forms the svastika posture.
With neck, head, and body held straight, one should constantly practice the Svastika posture;
in Gomukha, one should place the right ankle on the left side of the back.
Likewise on the right, the left [hand] is called gomukha;
one should grasp the lotus with both hands in reverse order, reaching as far as the thumbs.
O best of Brahmins, O wise one, by placing both soles of the feet upon the thighs, the *padmāsana* is formed; it removes all diseases and fear.
The heroic posture (*vīrāsana*):
one should place the two ankles below the scrotum on either side of the perineal seam;
the right ankle with the left [ankle], and likewise the other with the right. (6.1)
Placing his hands on his knees and extending his fingers, with a clear face and well-composed, he should gaze at the tip of his nose. (6.2)
This lion-throne is always worshipped by yogins.
In the Bhadrāsana posture, one should place the two ankles below the scrotum on either side of the perineum;
having firmly bound the feet against the sides with the hands, it should be made perfectly motionless.
This is the Bhadrāsana posture, which destroys poison and disease;
it is formed by pressing the thin seam of the perineum with the left ankle.
This is the *muktāsana*:
placing the left [foot] with its ankle over the right [thigh], and then placing the right ankle above that [left foot].
O Sage, having drawn the two ankles together, this is the *muktāsana*.
O best of sages, one should place the tips of the elbows at the sides of the navel; this is the *mayūrāsana*. (10)
Placing both palms upon the ground with a one-pointed mind, with his head and feet raised, he stood in the sky like a staff. || 11 ||
This is the peacock posture (mayūrāsana), which destroys all sins;
it is a comfortable posture by whatever means comfort and fortitude arise. || 12 ||
That is called a comfortable posture; one who is unable [to maintain other postures] should resort to it.
For one by whom the posture is mastered, the fruit of mastering the posture is attained; by him the three worlds are conquered. (13)
Endowed with this method, always perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus ends the third section;
the fourth section concerns the measurement of the body.
The body shall indeed measure ninety-six finger-breadths;
in the center of the body is the seat of fire, possessing the luster of molten gold. (1)
O Sāṃkṛti, the triangular [region] of human beings has indeed been truly described;
it is two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis.
(162) O Sāṃkṛti, know that for human beings the center of the body is the location of the *kanda*, nine finger-breadths from the *mūlādhāra*, O best of sages. (3)
O Bull among Sages, it should be four finger-breadths in length and width,
shaped like a hen’s egg, and adorned with skin and other such materials.
"O bull among sages, that which is called the 'navel' (nābhi) is situated in the midst of that [body], as declared by those who know yoga.

Since prāṇāyāma is accomplished through the body, its vital breaths, and the collection of channels (nāḍīs), the perfection of prāṇāyāma cannot occur without a thorough knowledge of the extent of the body and its functions."
He elaborates upon the dimensions of the body, the channels, and the vital breaths—beginning with "the body": "śikhisthāna" means the locus of fire. (1–10)
Regarding the enumeration of the channels:
the channel situated in the middle of the *kanda* is proclaimed as the *suṣumnā*. (5)
O bull among sages, seventy-two thousand channels stand surrounding it, of which fourteen are the principal ones.
Suṣumnā, Piṅgalā, likewise Iḍā and Sarasvatī;
Pūṣā, Varuṇā, Hastijihvā, and Yaśasvinī. || 7 ||
Alambusā, Kuhū, Viśvodārā, Payasvinī, Śaṅkhinī, and Gāndhārā—these are the fourteen principal [nāḍīs]. || 8 ||
Among these, three are the most principal, and among those three, one is the most excellent of the excellent;
O Sage, that is called the *brahmanāḍī* by the knowers of Vedānta.
O observer of excellent vows,
the Suṣumnā is firmly established from the backbone— consisting of the bones of the spinal column— up to the head.
(163) Regarding the location and nature of Kuṇḍalī:
"O Sage, the location of Kuṇḍalī is two finger-breadths below the root of the navel;
O best of sages, that Kuṇḍalī consists of the eightfold primordial nature."
Constantly restraining the movement of the winds as they truly are, as well as the water, food, and so forth,
she remains forever stationed around the sides of the *kanda*.
O Sage, having always enveloped the opening of the *brahmarandhra* with its own mouth, [the text] describes the location and nature of that *kuṇḍalinī* as follows: "at the navel," etc.
She consists of eight forms: earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego.
The primary dispositions. || 11–12 ||
Regarding the locations of the channels: Iḍā is situated on the left of the Suṣumnā, and Piṅgalā is on the right. || 13 ||
Sarasvatī and Kuhū are situated on the two sides of Suṣumnā;
Gāndhārā and Hastijihvā are on the back and front of Iḍā.
Pūṣā and Yaśasvinī are located on the back and the front of Piṅgalā; Kuha and Hastijihvā are on the sides, while Viśvodarā is situated in the middle.
Varuṇā is well-established in the middle of Yaśasvinī and Kuhū;
and Yaśasvinī is said to be between Pūṣā and Sarasvatī. (16)
Śaṅkhinī is said to be between Gāndhārī and Sarasvatī;
Alambusā is situated within the kanda, extending as far as the anus.
In the eastern part of the Suṣumṇā, Kuhū is situated within Rākā;
this channel is held to extend from below to above, reaching as far as the southern nostril.
O bull among sages, the iḍā is established at the end of the left nostril, and the yaśasvinī is held to extend to the big toe of the left foot. (19)
Pūṣan is said by the wise to extend from the edge of your left eye to the back of Piṅgalā, while Payasvinī extends to the edge of the right ear. || 20 ||
Likewise, O Sage, Sarasvatī goes upward as the tongue; and Hastijihvā is held to extend from the left big toe to the end of the tongue. (21)
The channel named Śaṅkhinī is held to extend to the left ear;
it is declared by the knowers of Vedānta that Gāndhārā extends to the left eye. (22)
The channel named Viśvodarā is situated in the middle of the kanda.
He states that the principal channels stand surrounding the Suṣumnā channel in the verse beginning with "suṣumnāyāḥ" (13–22).
The movement of the vital air within the channels consists of prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, samāna, and udāna.
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—these ten vital airs (vāyus) circulate through all the channels (nāḍīs). || 24 ||

Among them, O observer of noble vows, the five beginning with prāṇa are primary within the five [elements]. Among those two, O sage, that which is designated as prāṇa and apāna is to be honored as prāṇa.
O best of sages, the wind known as prāṇa always resides between the mouth and the nose, in the middle of the navel, and likewise in the heart.
O observer of noble vows, the *apāna* wind constantly moves within the middle of the anus, the thighs, and the knees;
throughout the entire abdomen, the hips, the navel, and the shanks. (27)
Vyāna resides between the ears and eyes, as well as at the two humps and the two ankles;
O bull among sages, it also exists in the throat, which is the seat of Prāṇa. (28)
The one known as Udāna is to be understood as being in the feet and the hands;
Samāna dwells pervading all bodies without doubt. (29)
The five winds, beginning with *nāga*, are situated within the skin, bones, and so forth.
He states that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and others move within these aforementioned channels (*nāḍī*) in the verse beginning with "prāṇa. (23) — These are the functions of the winds.
Exhalation, inhalation, and coughing—these indeed constitute the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa) in the realm of Sāṃkṛti.
The wind called apāna effects the discharge of feces, urine, and so forth; the samāna wind brings about proximity to all [the bodily constituents], O bull among sages. (31)
The udāna certainly causes upward movement; there is no doubt about this.
O Sage, the vyāna is declared by the knowers of Vedānta to be the cause of dispute.
O great sage, the quality of belching and so forth has been declared for the one named Nāga;
indeed, O son of Saṃkṛti, the function of Dhanañjaya is said to be beauty and the like.
O best of Brahmins, the closing [of the eyes] and so forth belong to Kūrma; hunger belongs to Kṛkara;
and the activity of drowsiness, O lord of sages, is proclaimed as belonging to Devadatta. (34)
He describes the functions of the ten vital airs, beginning with *prāṇa*, in the verses numbered 30–34, starting with the word "exhalation" (*niḥśvāsa*).
(166) The deities of the channels are as follows: Śiva is the deity of Suṣumṇā, Hari is the deity of Iḍā, Viriñca is the deity of Piṅgalā, and Virāj is the deity of Sarasvatī, O Sage. || 35 ||
Pūṣan is declared to be the presiding deity of [the nāḍī] Ādhidaivata; Varuṇa is the deity of Vāyu; and for the one named Hastijihvā, Varuṇa shall be the deity. (36)
O best of sages, the Lord Bhāskara is likewise [the son] of Yaśasvinī;
and Varuṇa, the essence of water, is proclaimed as the son of Alambuṣā. (37)
Kuhu is said to have Kṣud as its deity; Gāndhārī has Candra as its deity;
likewise, Śaṅkhinī has Candramas, and Payasvinī has Prajāpati. || 38 ||
The Lord Pāvaka is the husband of her who is named Viśvodarā.
He states the distinction between the deities of the fourteen channels, beginning with Suṣumnā, in the verse beginning with "suṣumnāyāḥ."
Regarding the movement of the moon and sun within the channels:
O great sage, the moon always moves within the iḍā channel. (39)
O Sage, best among the knowers of the Vedas, the sun likewise moves within Piṅgalā;
thus he says "In Iḍā," meaning that the moon and the sun move within both Iḍā and Piṅgalā. || 39 ||
Within the channels (nāḍīs), there is the movement of the Sun, which is the vital breath (prāṇa) consisting of the year; furthermore, there is the transition of the wind from Piṅgalā into Iḍā. (40)
O Sage, that is declared as the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) by those who know the Vedānta;
it is the transference of the vital breath from the iḍā into the piṅgalā, O Sage. (41)
"The southern course is said to be in the Piṅgalā," so says the Śruti. When the vital breath (prāṇa) arrives at the junction of the Iḍā and the Piṅgalā, [that is the time]. (42)
Then, O best among embodied beings, that is declared to be the new moon (amāvasyā) within the body;
when the vital breath has entered the mūlādhāra, O most excellent of scholars. (43)
O best of ascetics, that was declared by the practitioners of austerity to be the first equinox;
O foremost of sages, it was called "Prāṇa" when [the breath] entered the head.
That final equinox is proclaimed by the ascetics who contemplate reality;
the transition of all the months occurs through inhalation and exhalation. (45)
O best among the knowers of reality, when the vital breath (prāṇa) reaches the seat of Kuṇḍalinī through the iḍā [nāḍī], that is called the "eclipse of the moon" (somagrahaṇa). 46.
O best of sages, whenever the vital breath (prāṇa) reaches the seat of Kuṇḍalinī by means of Piṅgalā, at that very moment there occurs a solar eclipse.

He says that the days, fortnights, months, solstices, and so forth, as well as the calculation of the planets, arise from the movement of the channels (*nāḍī*) and zodiac signs (*rāśi*) of the Sun, which is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose nature is the year—thus [he says]: "Of Piṅgalā" (verse 40).
[This concludes] the praise of the internal sacred sites (*antastīrtha*).
O one of great wisdom, Śrīparvata is in the place of the head, Kedāra on the forehead, and Vārāṇasī between the eyebrows and the nose.
Kurukṣetra is in the region of the breasts, Prayāga is in the lotus of the heart;
the sky of consciousness (cidambara) is in the center of the heart, and the abode of Kamalā is in the foundation (ādhāra).
He who abandons the sacred ford of the Self and goes to external fords is like one who, having cast away the great jewel held in his hand, seeks glass. (50)
The state of being (bhāva) is the supreme sacred ford, the authority in all actions;
for in one way a beloved wife is embraced, and in another way a daughter.
Yogins do not resort to sacred fords filled with water or to deities fashioned from wood and other materials, because they possess the conviction of their own Self.
O great sage, the supreme sacred ford is within, not outside;
the sacred ford of the Self is the great sacred ford—any other sacred ford is useless.
A mind that is corrupted within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords;
it remains as impure as a wine-vessel even after being washed with water a hundred times. (54)
At the times of the equinoxes and solstices, during eclipses, and always on special occasions, a man becomes pure by bathing in a place such as Vāraṇasī.

O best of sages, for those ignorant ones who are devoted to the yoga of knowledge, the water used for washing their feet serves as a sacred bathing place for the purification of their inner disposition.
He states that the sacred sites such as Śrīśaila exist from the head down to the base of the support:

"Śrīparvata" (verse 48–49). Thus, he praises this very self-purifying holy site (*ātmatīrtha*) consisting of meditative realization, which should be resorted to by those seeking liberation: "The self-purifying holy site" (verse 50). [He compares] glass to a glass-gem (*kācamaṇi*).

The meaning is that regarding all actions performed by means of the body and so forth, the perception of them as sacred fords (*tīrtha*) is most excellent. In this regard, the illustration is: "Otherwise... (verse 51). For this very reason, [it is said] "thus, the sacred fords" (verse 52). That alone is the "sacred ford of the Self" (verse 53). No one becomes pure by bathing in external sacred fords.
He states this with an illustration: "The mind... (verse 54). He says that it is not so by bathing at a sacred ford (*bhāvatīrtha*): (p.

169) the meaning is that through the continuous contemplation of one's own Self as the objective mark (*lakṣya*) in locations such as the space between the eyebrows, one becomes the pure Self alone. (verse 55)
Thus, he says "jñāna... [verse 56], stating that one who is ineligible for bathing at the sacred ford of the Self becomes pure through contact with the water from the feet of the Tīrtha-pāda.
The deluded soul always perceives Śiva in the self, in sacred fords, in charity, in recitation, in sacrifice, in wood, and in stone; yet he fails to see Śiva established within his own body. 57.
He who abandons me who dwells within and serves that which is outside is like one who discards a morsel of food held in his own hand and licks his elbow. 58.
Yogins do not perceive Śiva in images;
images have been fashioned for the sake of the meditation of the ignorant. (59)

Those who do not know themselves (svājñaḥ) desire to see a self other than their own, whereas those who know themselves (svajñāḥ) perceive their very Self; thus he says: "In the sacred ford" (tīrthe). (Verses 57–58) For this very reason, it is called "Auspicious" (śivam).
Out of compassion for those who are not practitioners of yoga, even an image is conceptualized; thus he says: "Of the ignorant" (ajñānām). (Verse 59)

Through the vision of Brahman, one attains the state of Brahman—the unprecedented, unsurpassed Brahman, one’s own Self, which is Truth, non-dual, a mass of consciousness, and bliss; he who sees thus, truly sees. 60.
O Great Sage, having completely cast off this human state—which is a mere mass of channels and always unsubstantial—realize the Self by means of the self, thinking "I am [that]. (61)
Having realized the bodiless one within bodies, the great, all-pervading Lord, the imperishable bliss itself— the wise man does not grieve.
When the ignorance that produces differentiation has been destroyed by the power of knowledge, O sage, what can it do to the unreal distinction between the self and Brahman? (63)
He says that he who perceives Brahman as without distinction becomes that very thing itself:

"That which is without prior" (*apūrvam*). Since there exists no cause prior to it nor any effect subsequent to it, he who perceives that Brahman—which is devoid of the conceptualization of cause and effect—is his own self alone; he [becomes that].

The meaning is that only that [the Self] remains. (60) As long as there is no purity of mind, one should practice yoga with the contemplation of being a human; then, when purity has arisen, one should abandon the state of being a human and abide in the state of Brahman—thus he says: "The channels... (61). He who...
He says that whoever knows the Self in this way becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done: "The bodiless," and so forth.

62 || He says that when the perception of difference born of one's own ignorance has vanished, Brahman remains as undivided: "vibheda... (verse 63). What can difference do, which is in reality impossible even throughout the three periods of time? The meaning is that because its own nature has been attained, Brahman remains as undivided. 63 ||
Thus ends the fourth section;
the fifth section: Purification of the Channels.

O Brahmin, explain to me correctly and in brief the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi), by means of which purification, constantly meditating, I may become liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 1 ||
O Sāṅkṛti, listen; I shall explain the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi) in brief.
One who is engaged in the rites prescribed by the injunctions and is free from desire and mental constructs [should practice it]. || 2 ||
He who is endowed with the eightfold restraint, peaceful, devoted to truth, firmly established in his own self, and well-instructed by those possessed of perfect knowledge; (3)
On a mountain peak, by a riverbank, at the foot of a *bilva* tree, or in a forest—having constructed a hermitage in a delightful and pure place, one should remain composed. (4)
Then, having taken his seat facing either east or north,
with his neck, head, and body held straight, his mouth closed, and remaining perfectly motionless— (5)
With eyes well-composed, one should behold the fourth state (turīya) as nectar flowing from the center of the drop within the lunar orb at the tip of the nose.
Having drawn in the breath through the *iḍā* and filled it within the belly,
one should then meditate upon the fire situated in the center of the body, accompanied by a mass of flames.
The wise one should contemplate the seed-syllable of fire (Ra) conjoined with the Bindu and Nāda;
thereafter, he should properly exhale the vital breath through the Piṅgalā.
Again, having filled [the body] through the Piṅgalā, one should contemplate the seed-syllable of fire;
then the wise one should exhale slowly and gradually through the Iḍā alone.
Or for three or four days, or indeed three or four times;
one should always wander thus six times during the three junctions of the day in secret.
He asks with the desire to know the purification of the channels cultivated through the human state; thus he says:
"Properly" (samyak). The Blessed One gives the answer to the question: "O son of Saṅkṛti" (sāṃkṛta).
Regarding the question "Of what kind is that?", [the author] says: "Stated as an injunction" (vidhyukta). (2.5)
The meaning is that one should commence the yoga while gazing at the tip of the nose at the lunar disc from which nectar is flowing.
(6–7) "Rām" is the seed-syllable of fire. (8–9) Three or four times every day. (10–14, p.
172) [The signs of the purification of the channels.]
One attains the purification of the channels, characterized by distinct signs:
lightness of the body and the radiance of the digestive fire residing within the stomach.
The manifestation of the inner sound (nāda) is the sign that indicates its perfection;
as long as one perceives these, one should practice in this manner. || 12 ||
Purification of one's own self:
Alternatively, having abandoned this [external ritual], one should practice the purification of one's own self;
for the Self is eternally pure, constant, of the nature of bliss, and self-luminous. (13)
Through ignorance this [Self] appears stained; through knowledge it shines forth as pure.
He who washes away the mud of the impurity of ignorance with the water of knowledge is alone ever pure; no other is so, for he is merely devoted to ritual action.
Thus ends the fifth section;
the sixth section is on the characteristics of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
O Sāṃkṛti, listen with respect as I describe the sequence of prāṇāyāma;
it is defined as such by means of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka). || 1 ||
Exhalation, inhalation, and retention are said to consist of the three phonemes (varṇas). This is declared to be the Praṇava, and prāṇāyāma is composed of that.
Having drawn in the breath through the *iḍā* and filled it so that it resides in the abdomen, one should slowly meditate upon the syllable *A* there for sixteen measures (*mātrā*). (3)
After filling it, one should hold [the breath] for sixty-four *mātrās*,
while here too recollecting the form of the syllable *U* and muttering the *praṇava*.
Or, as long as one is able, the wise person, intent on recitation, should retain the breath; thereafter, when it is full, he should exhale the air with the syllable *ma*.
Again, this breath control (prāṇāyāma) performed slowly by Piṅgalā with thirty-two measures (mātrās) should be practiced in that manner. || 6 ||
Again, having filled [the breath] with sixteen measures by means of Piṅgalā,
one should likewise meditate here upon the form of the syllable *A* with a one-pointed mind.
The wise and self-controlled practitioner, while reciting the Praṇava,
should retain the filled [breath] for sixty-four mātrās, meditating upon the form of the syllable *U*.
Then, while recollecting the syllable *ma*, one should exhale the breath through the *iḍā* [left nostril];
in this very same manner, the wise man should act again, filling [the breath] through the *iḍā*.
O Lord of Sages, one should thus constantly practice *prāṇāyāma* in this manner;
by practicing it regularly in this way, one becomes possessed of knowledge within six months.
Within a year one becomes a knower of Brahman; therefore, one should practice constantly.
He who is always devoted to the practice of yoga and ever intent upon his own duty [attains this]. || 11 ||
By the very restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), one will become liberated through knowledge;
this is especially so in the case of breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 1-11 ||
The definition of *pūraka* and the others:
the filling of the external air into the stomach is indeed *pūraka*. (12)
The retention of breath like a full pitcher is known as *kumbhaka*;
the expulsion of air from the abdomen is remembered as *recaka*. || 13 ||
He states the characteristics of *pūraka* and the others [the breath-retention techniques] beginning with the words "from the external" (*bāhyāt*). || 12–13 ||
Among the perfections of *prāṇāyāma*, that which produces perspiration is the lowest;
one should know that trembling is the middling, and rising [into the air] is known as the highest. (14)
One should perform each preceding stage until the capacity for rising [to the next] arises;
when the highest stage is possible, the wise man shall become happy through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
O observer of noble vows, by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the mind indeed becomes pure;
when the mind is pure, one becomes truly purified and established in the inner light (pratyagjyotis). || 16 ||
The vital breath, conjoined with the mind, abides in the Supreme Self of this great-souled person who is devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). 17.
By that, the body rises up; from some degree of knowledge comes liberation.
Abandoning exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), one should practice the retention (kumbhaka) of consciousness. 18.
Freed from all evil, he shall attain perfect knowledge;
he gains the speed of thought, and his grey hair and other such signs of aging perish.
For one who is solely devoted to *prāṇāyāma*, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain.
Therefore, one should practice *prāṇāyāmas* with every effort. (20)
He states the accomplishment of perspiration and so forth: "prasveda... (14–17). [The yogi] rises from the surface of the earth.
O observer of noble vows, I shall now declare the specific applications of the various types of *prāṇāyāma* that remove disease:
[they should be performed] at the two junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*), during the time sacred to Brahmā (*brāhmakāla*), or always at midday.
Having drawn in the external breath and filled it within the belly, by means of concentration (dhāraṇā) upon the tip of the nose, the center of the navel, and the big toe of the foot; || 22 ||
Freed from all diseases, a man shall live for a hundred years; or, by means of concentration on the tip of the nose, he becomes a conqueror of the senses, O observer of noble vows. (23)
By holding [the breath] at the center of the navel, there shall be the cessation of all diseases;
O Brahmin, by restraining the big toe, the body becomes light.
The man who, having drawn in the wind with his tongue, drinks it constantly, becomes free from fatigue and burning heat; such a yogi shall attain freedom from disease. (25)
Having drawn in the air with the tongue, one should restrain it at the root of the tongue;
drinking the nectar without distraction, one shall attain complete happiness. (26)
Having drawn in the vital air through the *iḍā*, one should restrain it between the eyebrows;
he who drinks this pure nectar is indeed liberated from diseases. (27)

O knower of the essence of the Vedas, one should restrain [the breath] at the navel by means of both the *iḍā* and the *piṅgalā* through the secret doctrine of yoga; by that, a person is liberated from diseases. (28)
For one month, at the three junctions of the day, having placed the breath upon the tongue,
and drinking the nectar, one should very gently restrain it at the navel.
The disorders born of Vāta and Pitta are undoubtedly destroyed;
having drawn in the breath through both nostrils, one should restrain it within the pair of eyes. (30)
Thus eye diseases are destroyed by the closing of the ears;
likewise, having directed the breath upward, one should hold it as it remains in the head. (31)
"Head diseases are destroyed; this has indeed been spoken truly, O Sāṃkṛti.

He now states the different types of *dhāraṇā* which eliminate those diseases that are obstacles to the attainment of yoga, beginning with the word "viniyogān" (applications). "At the time of Brahmā" means during the *brāhma-muhūrta*. (21–35)
The conquest of the vital air is achieved through the practice of the Ṣaṇmukhī-mudrā and other means, while remaining seated in the Svastika posture with a concentrated mind. || 32 ||
Having raised the downward breath (apāna) upward by means of the syllable Om (praṇava) very slowly,
one should properly hold both the primary and secondary organs with the two hands.
O Sage, having covered the ears with the two thumbs, the eyes with the two index fingers, and the nostrils with the other two fingers, one should indeed conceal the sense organs.
O great sage, as long as bliss manifests, one should maintain [the breath] at the crown of the head; by this very means, the vital breath (prāṇa) proceeds to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
When the vital air has reached the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), O sinless one, a sound arises;
at first it resembles the sound of a conch, and in the middle it is like the rumbling of clouds. (36)
When the vital air has entered the center of the head like a spring flowing from a mountain,
O highly wise one, you shall afterwards become joyful and directly oriented toward the Self.
Furthermore, through that yoga, the perfection of that knowledge occurs and the concealment of saṃsāra takes place.
One should firmly press the *sīvinī* with the right and left ankles. (38)
A wise man, mindful of the three-eyed god, should press with his left ankle the joint situated below the knees.
O Sage, having again called to mind Vināyaka and likewise Vāgīśvarī,
one should draw forth the wind from the base of the *liṅga* and place it before oneself.
O best of Brahmins, the wise man, by means of the Praṇava joined with the Bindu, should restrain that [breath] in the center of the Mūlādhāra. || 41 ||
Having been kindled by the wind and suppressed, the fire ascends the Kuṇḍalinī;
then the wind proceeds again through the Suṣumṇā together with the fire.
For one who practices in this manner, the vital air (vāyu) becomes thoroughly conquered.
Thus, through the practice of the Ṣaṇmukhī-mudrā, [the breath reaches] the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). Just so, from the mountain of the lunar orb, a stream of nectar arises; by that—
Having consecrated the light-liṅga situated between the eyebrows, the yogin becomes free from death by tasting that nectar. Thereafter, pressing with his two right and left ankles the *sīvinī*—
the channel located between the genitals and the anus— at the joint situated below the knees...
Having recollected Śivaliṅga and having meditated upon Vināyaka and Vāgīśvarī, [he recites] "Then from the navel of the Liṅga," and so forth. (Verses 39–42)
(178) O best of sages, the signs of mastery over the vital winds are first perspiration, followed by trembling.
And the ability to raise the body is a sign when the breath has been conquered.
He describes the signs indicating mastery over the vital air (vāyu) as follows: "perspiration," and so forth. (Verses 43–48).
Through mastery over the vital air (vāyu), there arises knowledge preceded by the destruction of disease, sin, and dispassion;
for him who practices in this manner, the root disease perishes. || 44 ||
O Sāṃkṛti, Bhagaṃdhara shall be destroyed, as shall all diseases;
both minor and major sins will perish.
When evil has perished, the wondrous mirror of the mind becomes pure;
once again, detachment from the enjoyments of Brahmā and the other gods arises within the heart.
But for one who is detached from worldly existence, knowledge is the means to liberation;
by knowing the god Sadāśiva, there shall be the destruction of the bonds.
He by whom the nectar-like essence of knowledge has been tasted even once, abandons all other activities and runs toward that alone. (48)
The wise declare that this world is indeed of the nature of consciousness;
others of perverted vision, due to ignorance, perceive it as having the nature of external objects. (49)
Through the realization of the true nature of the self, ignorance is completely destroyed;
O one of great wisdom, when ignorance is destroyed, passion and the other afflictions are likewise destroyed. (50)
O wise one, when passion and the like no longer arise, there is an investigation into merit and demerit;
upon the destruction of those two, one is no longer joined with a body. (51)
The wise are those possessed of knowledge. (49–50) "Vimarśana" means purification, that is to say, destruction. (51)
Thus ends the sixth section.
The seventh section concerns the definition of Pratyāhāra and its varieties.
Now, therefore, O great sage, I shall fully explain withdrawal (pratyāhāra) regarding the sense organs that wander among their objects by their very nature. (1)
The forceful withdrawal of those [senses] is called pratyāhāra;
for one who is concentrated, seeing everything as Brahman, whatever he sees, he sees as Brahman. (2)
This is what is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra), as previously taught by the knowers of Brahman:
whatever one performs until the end of life, whether it be pure or impure. (3)
One should offer all that to Brahman; that is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Alternatively, one may perform the daily obligatory rites with the intention of worshipping Brahman.
One should likewise perform the optional [practices]; that is called pratyāhāra (withdrawal).
Alternatively, having drawn in the breath, one should restrain it from place to place.

Likewise, having drawn the breath from the roots of the teeth into the wooden stick, then from the throat into the chest, and from the region of the chest, one should restrain it at the region of the navel.
Having drawn [the breath] upward from the region of the navel, one should restrain it within the Kuṇḍalinī;
from the region of the Kuṇḍalinī, the wise man should restrain it in the Mūlādhāra. (7)
Then, O slender-waisted one, one should restrain the downward breath at the two hips, as well as the thighs; from there, at the two knees, the shanks, and the big toes.
This withdrawal (pratyāhāra) was indeed described in the past by those devoted to withdrawal.

Having established the extent of restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), and breath control (prāṇāyāma), he then states the essential nature of withdrawal with the words "Now" (atha). (1.12)
Such is the fruit of withdrawal for that great-souled person who is thus engaged in practice. || 9 ||
O observer of noble vows, all sins and the disease of worldly existence are destroyed through pratyāhāra consisting of the retention of breath (vāyudhāraṇā).
Drawing the breath through both nostrils while remaining motionless in the svastika posture, one should practice.
The wise one should fill the vital air from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
afterwards, he should do the same for both feet and likewise for the *mūlādhāra*.
One should fix [the mind] upon the navel-center, the middle of the heart, the root of the throat, the palate,
the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, and likewise upon the crown of the head.
The withdrawal (pratyāhāra) approved by the Vedānta:

Having drawn back the notion of self from the body, the wise man, being composed, should dissolve it within the Self—within the Self that is free from dualities and beyond conceptual construction. 13.
(181) Pratyāhāra has been thus fully explained by those who truly know the Vedānta.
For one who practices in this manner, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain. (14)
What more need be said?—"In the body," [it is said]. (13–14)
Thus ends the seventh section.
The eighth section:
concentration on the five elements.
Now, therefore, O observer of noble vows, I shall fully explain the five dhāraṇās:
one should fix the external space within the void situated in the center of the body. || 1 ||
In the vital breath, one should likewise [dissolve] the external air; in the fire, the digestive fire within the stomach;
in the watery portion, water; and in the earthy portion, O great sage, the earth.
One should recite the mantra known as Hayarāvalakāra in sequence;
this is declared to be the supreme concentration (dhāraṇā), which purifies all sins.

The portion of the earth extends to the knees; the portion of the waters is said to extend to the feet; likewise, the portion of fire extends to the heart, and the portion of air extends to the midpoint between the eyebrows. || 4 ||
O wise one, the portion of space is likewise proclaimed to be the head;
Brahmā resides in the portion of earth, and Viṣṇu in the portion of water.
One should meditate on Maheśāna in the portion of fire, Īśvara in the portion of wind,
and Sadāśiva, O one of great wisdom, in the portion of space.
Having stated the definition of *pratyāhāra*, he now states the definition of *dhāraṇā*: "Now," etc. (p.
182): "O bull among sages, I shall now tell you of *dhāraṇā* either with respect to the Self (*ātman*) or [with respect to other objects]."
Within the Puruṣa, one should contemplate Śiva, the teacher of all, who consists of the bliss of awakening.
The wise person should constantly maintain this for the purification of all sins,
having withdrawn the effects, such as Brahmā and the others, each into their respective causes.
One should fix the mind directly upon the complete Self within the *praṇava*, which is the cause of all, unmanifest, indefinable, and insentient;
having withdrawn the senses, one should unite the mind with the Self. (9)

One should maintain the auspicious (Śiva) within the inward-facing Person (puruṣa), by virtue of its swallowing all that is other than itself; or alternatively, one should maintain the inward-facing one, who is the ruler of all, within the Person, that is, the Supreme Self. || 7–9 ||
Thus ends the eighth section.
The ninth section:
Meditation on Brahman with its residual attributes (*saviśeṣa-brahma-dhyāna*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim meditation, which destroys saṃsāra;
it is the eternal truth, the supreme Brahman, and the medicine for all worldly existence. (1)
With great reverence, one should meditate upon Maheśvara— the Lord of the Lords of Yogins— who is the one of upward-spilling semen, Virūpākṣa, and Viśvarūpa, thinking "I am He."
Having stated the *dhāraṇā*, he describes the meditation (*dhyāna*) on Brahman with and without attributes, beginning with "Now" (*atha*).
*Ṛtam* is the fruit of action, the lower Brahman; *satyam* is the fruit of knowledge, the higher Brahman.

p. 183) Or else, [one should practice] meditation on Brahman devoid of distinctions—that which is the true Lord, knowledge, bliss, non-dual, exceedingly pure, eternal, and free from beginning, middle, and end. || 3 ||
Likewise, it is not gross, not space-like, intangible, and beyond the range of sight;
it possesses neither taste nor what is called smell, and is immeasurable and incomparable.
O observer of noble vows, for the sake of liberation, one should meditate upon the Self as the infinite Brahman— being, consciousness, and bliss— transcending the body, thinking, "I am this."
It is called "atyartha" because it exists as mere cognition (jñaptimātratayā), having transcended the collection of objects (arthajātam). || 3 ||
By means of the five qualifiers beginning with "not space" (anākāśa), its distinction from the five elements is stated. || 4-6 ||
For a great-souled person thus engaged in the practice of the fruit of meditation,
the realization of Vedānta will arise in due course; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the ninth section;
the tenth section: the nature of samādhi.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the samādhi that destroys worldly existence;
samādhi is the arising of pure consciousness regarding the oneness of the supreme Self and the individual soul.
The Self is indeed eternal, omnipresent, immutable, and free from defects;
though it is one, it appears divided through delusion and *māyā*, but not by its own nature.
Therefore, only non-duality exists; there is neither the phenomenal world nor transmigratory existence.
Just as space is spoken of as "the space within a jar" or "the space within a hut. (3)
Thus, by the deluded, the Self is described in two ways as the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara):
"I am neither the body, nor the vital breath, nor the senses, nor indeed the mind. (4)
"O best of sages, that state of mind which realizes, 'I am indeed Śiva alone, because I am eternally of the nature of the witness,' is here called samādhi. (5)
Having explained the types of meditative absorption (dhyāna), he states the types of concentration (samādhi) with the words "Now" (atha). 1–2.
Since this is so, therefore: just as the space within a jar is indeed [identical to] space itself. (3-6)
I am that which remains as pure Brahman; I am Brahman, not a transmigrating being, and never anything other than Me.
Just as foam, waves, and the like arise from the ocean and [return to it] again... (6)
Just as [the water] dissolves into the ocean, so too the world dissolves into that which consists of the world;
therefore, the mind does not exist separately, nor indeed does the illusion of the world exist.
He for whom this Supreme Self is revealed as the innermost self attains the state of a person and becomes himself the manifest Supreme Immortality.
When consciousness shines eternally and universally within the mind,
then it is spontaneously attained by the yogi without obstruction.
When one perceives all beings within one's own self, and the self within all beings, then one attains Brahman. (10)
When one established in meditative absorption does not perceive any beings, having become one with the Supreme, then he becomes absolute. (11)
When one perceives the self as absolute in the ultimate sense,
and the entire world as mere illusion, then there is liberation.
Since this is so, therefore the mind does not exist apart from me. || 7 ||

"Because of the oneness of the inner and outer consciousness, [it is] 'by itself' (svayam), etc."—the meaning culminating in the *Darśanopaniṣad* is this: when the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) beyond one's own self has reached the state of being mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), there remains only the non-dual Brahman alone, by itself. (8–12)
Conclusion: Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the great sage Dattātreya, the son of Saṅkṛti, remained happily and utterly fearless in his own true nature. 13.
Thus [it is said].
He concludes the narrative with the word "evam" (thus). The word "iti" is for the purpose of marking the completion of the Darśanopaniṣad. || 13 ||
Thus ends the tenth section. The commentary on the Darśanopaniṣad, which culminates in Brahman alone, has been written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The commentary on the Darśanopaniṣad is recorded as consisting of two hundred [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Darśanopaniṣad, completing the ninety-first [treatise] in the commentary on the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the ŚrīmadĪśa.
